prior_narrative.tldr: This thread is a reading list of LLM research grouped by shared wording, not one event. From Oct 29 it ran through self-learning, pruning, Anthropic's Nov 2 provable-inference update and knowledge editing to Nov 10-13 work on what eval scores measure and when a model should abstain or ask for clarification.
prior_narrative.whats_new: Nov 16: TRIAGE-CPG compares LLMs deciding under a budget whether to clear, flag or escalate unknown binaries, and dhAIBench benchmarks LLMs for linguistic annotation under documented conditions.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: Most items are single unreplicated preprints, but the recent run converges on a production question: when a model should answer, ask, abstain or escalate, and how to measure that decision rather than raw accuracy.

beats.headline: Keeping models current: RL-driven self-learning beyond plain RAG
beats.summary: Opens the window with knowledge acquisition coupled to reasoning in unfamiliar domains.

beats.headline: Efficiency work: extreme-sparsity pruning and an early-stopping audit for reasoning models
beats.summary: A text-to-SQL architecture survey lands the same day.

beats.headline: Anthropic reports progress on zkSNARK-based provable inference
beats.summary: The thread's only lab-published item: cryptographic proofs applied to LLM inference.

beats.headline: Updating what models know: answerability drift, multimodal unlearning and lifelong knowledge editing
beats.summary: Also here: an LLM choosing federated aggregation rules without training.

beats.headline: Judgment under scrutiny: rising rater standards on Chatbot Arena, framing effects and personality benchmarks
beats.summary: These days also bring an LLM AutoML searcher, physics-guided fault diagnosis, a training-simulation benchmark and a cognitive account of learning by thinking.

beats.headline: What do scores measure? ShadowBench and a corrupted-input study probe shortcuts behind passing evals
beats.summary: One tests recall without explicit entity names; the other asks whether LLMs pass NLI on noun-stripped or shuffled inputs.

beats.headline: Knowing when not to answer: black-box uncertainty and an interactive ambiguity-resolution eval
beats.summary: One splits prompt ambiguity from knowledge gaps via API calls only; the other scores when a model should ask versus assume. A tabular anomaly-detection paper lands the same day.

beats.headline: Applied decisions: budgeted malware triage, annotation benchmarking and a survey of LLMs for AI infrastructure
beats.summary: The newest items move from model internals to LLMs making operational calls under cost and documentation constraints.

open_questions: Does TRIAGE-CPG report which models escalate too rarely or too often under a fixed analysis budget?
Does the ensemble-of-ensembles method report how many model calls per prompt it needs, and how that compares with deep ensembles?
Does the ambiguity-resolution eval show models asking for clarification at the right rate, or defaulting to assumptions?
Do published unlearning or knowledge-editing methods still pass when probed without explicit entity names, as ShadowBench suggests they may not?
Do Chatbot Arena or other human-preference leaderboards adjust rankings for the rater drift the Nov 10 study describes?
Does Anthropic publish proving cost or latency figures for zkSNARK-based provable inference?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: Score your agent's answer/ask/abstain/escalate decisions as a separate eval with perturbed controls (renamed entities, shuffled inputs), and measure the per-request call cost of any uncertainty method before wiring it into routing.

storylines.label: Multi-Agent Systems
storylines.latest_title: Kaer: Security-Aware Replanning for Multi-Agent Systems

prior_narrative.tldr: This is a loose research cluster, not one event: September papers framed multi-agent systems as a shared-state problem (memory graphs, handoffs, latent channels). Since Oct 28 the work has split into orchestration benchmarks, security and privacy controls, failure attribution, and memory cost.
prior_narrative.whats_new: The newest item, a Nov 17 InfoQ talk on how LinkedIn distilled a 7B ranking model to 400M parameters to meet P99 latency SLAs, is a serving-cost case study rather than a multi-agent result.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: The open problems in multi-agent stacks have moved from how to coordinate to how to secure, debug, and pay for them: agent identity, data leakage, which agent caused a failure, and KV-cache memory per resident agent.

beats.headline: Papers attack fixed workflows: self-evolving orchestrators, information gaps, and a benchmark
beats.summary: MAS-Loop learns orchestration from repeated runs, a gap-locating method fixes communication graphs that hide evidence, and WorkflowArena benchmarks executable worker-spawning workflows.

beats.headline: Security and privacy become the dominant thread, from NIST guidance to an open-source leak tester
beats.summary: Auditable belief updates, NIST identity tenets, private retrieval, secure aggregation against malicious agents, and AgentLeak all target what one agent can see, claim, or leak.

beats.headline: CoLFA traces a failure to the decisive step and the responsible agent
Memory and serving cost: coordinated KV-cache quantization, agent-designed serving, LinkedIn's distillation
beats.summary: Only the KV-cache paper is multi-agent-specific; ServerBench and the LinkedIn talk are adjacent serving work the clustering pulled in.

open_questions: Does any open-source agent framework adopt per-agent identity along the lines of NIST's design tenets?
Does AgentLeak gain users or published results against real frameworks beyond its Show HN launch?
Does WorkflowArena get adopted as a shared orchestration benchmark by other papers?
Does coordinated KV-cache quantization ship in a serving engine that hosts several agents per GPU?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: Give each agent its own identity and scoped credentials, and log which agent produced each step, so failures and leaks can be attributed; treat the orchestration and quantization papers as research until they are replicated.

storylines.label: Recursive Self-Improvement
storylines.latest_title: Piccolo: Co-Evolving Decision Models and Data through Recursive Self-Improvement

prior_narrative.tldr: Three papers in two weeks each propose a concrete recursive self-improvement (RSI) mechanism: a system that observes its own performance and converts that evidence into its next round of training. The pattern started with a general agentic post-training framework, then moved into domain-specific self-evolution loops for medical agents and AI research agents.
prior_narrative.whats_new: The newest paper (Sep 22) applies RSI to AI research agents automating their own R&D -- training efficiency and inference optimization -- rather than a fixed task domain.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: If an agent framework can retrain on its own output, your eval suite needs to catch capability drift in the feedback loop itself, not just score the model's latest checkpoint.

beats.headline: NeoHorse-1 proposes a routing-harness mechanism for RSI via agentic post-training
beats.summary: First concrete mechanism for how a system converts observed capability into the next training round.

beats.headline: Self-evolution loops extend to medical agents and AI research agents
beats.summary: The same RSI pattern reapplied to clinically aligned medical agents, then to agents automating AI R&D itself.

open_questions: Do any of these RSI mechanisms hold up outside benchmark/simulation settings, or only in the papers' own eval harnesses?
Does the self-improvement loop compound capability faster than the evaluation methodology can track it?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: Before trusting a framework's self-improvement claim, ask what concrete signal it retrains on and how that signal is audited independently of the system generating it.

storylines.label: Continual Learning
storylines.latest_title: Hypnos: A Dual-Phase End-to-End Platform for Scalable Continual Learning at the Edge

prior_narrative.tldr: An Oct 22 paper (HERD) framed continual learning as a trade-off between parametric methods, which forget, and non-parametric ones. A benchmark followed on Oct 25 for whether LLM agents improve from experience, then CAMR on Oct 27 for choosing what to replay.
prior_narrative.whats_new: Oct 28: Routed Continual Learning lets deployed agents share experience, routing among retention mechanisms rather than relying on a single one.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: Agents that learn from experience need retention without regressions; replay selection, long-horizon evals and now cross-agent sharing are the pieces to watch.

status.detail: Four arXiv papers in seven days; all research-stage, none shipped in a product.

beats.headline: HERD targets forgetting with recursive distillation
beats.summary: Positions parametric methods against catastrophic forgetting and loss of plasticity.

beats.headline: Continual Learning Exam benchmarks LLM agents over long horizons
CAMR selects what to replay by compatibility
Routed Continual Learning shares experience across agents

open_questions: Do any labs report results on the Continual Learning Exam benchmark?
Do HERD, CAMR or Routed Continual Learning release code or reproducible numbers on production-scale models?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: Treat these as research signals: do not adopt, but add a retention check to any fine-tune or agent-memory pipeline that updates on new data.

prior_narrative.tldr: This is a loose cluster of mostly arXiv papers that share policy- and preference-optimization vocabulary, not one developing story. It began with RL recipes for agents, preference-optimization variants and kernel-tuning agents, then drifted toward vision-language hallucination fixes and benchmarks for visual agents.
prior_narrative.whats_new: Nov 18: Einsia AI announced Visual Cipher Bench for long-horizon visual reasoning in agents, joining PhysScope and MM-ReportBench in a week of multimodal-agent evaluation work.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: If you ship agents that read screens, diagrams or images, the evidence here is about grounding failures (answering from priors instead of the pixels), and every result is author-reported on the papers' own benchmarks, not production evidence.

beats.headline: RL recipes target the hard parts of training agents: delayed credit, orchestration and partial verifiers
beats.summary: TSBPO, few-step flow RL, CRESiST for speech translation, learned multi-agent orchestration, and negative-only policy optimization.

beats.headline: Preference-optimization papers target general preferences, shifting objectives, noisy labels and missing gold answers
beats.summary: DNO empirical study, preference learning from multi-agent debate, steerable multi-objective GRPO with LoRA adapters, and PORT token reweighting.

beats.headline: Agents that tune GPU kernels and AI infrastructure get methods and benchmarks
beats.summary: Question-driven kernel agents, a local 7B CUDA study, Infrathon, and the Ascend NPU benchmark AscendGYM.

beats.headline: The cluster shifts to vision-language models that hallucinate objects or reason past what they see
beats.summary: MIRA, latent multimodal reasoning, VIGOR, cross-modal unlearning, VEPO, GEM-MM and severity-aware preference validation.

beats.headline: Optimization papers on routing, merchandising and federated learning ride along on shared vocabulary
beats.summary: Small-model capability routing, cold-start cover-photo selection, parallel split learning, and explainable federated learning.

beats.headline: Visual-agent benchmarks pile up: decoys, web tasks, physics diagrams, reports and cipher puzzles
beats.summary: Elorian's decoy test, Google's Multimodal Knowledge Agent Benchmark, Vision-as-a-Tool, WebArena-Pro, ViRA, MM-ReportBench, PhysScope and Visual Cipher Bench.

open_questions: Does any independent group reproduce TSBPO's gains on long-horizon agent tasks outside the paper's own environments?
Does negative-only policy optimization train useful agents when the verifier can only reject wrong answers in real tool-use settings?
Do kernel-optimization agents beat vendor libraries and hand-tuned kernels on Infrathon or AscendGYM workloads under their cost accounting?
Do the VLM hallucination fixes (VEPO, GEM-MM, severity-aware alignment) hold up on screenshots and documents rather than natural photos?
Will Visual Cipher Bench publish tasks, scoring code and model results, or stay an announcement?
Does external visual tooling (Vision-as-a-Tool, zooming in ViRA) beat a stronger base model's own vision on WebArena-Pro-style tasks?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: If your agent reads screens or images, add eval cases where the obvious prior answer is wrong (decoys, altered diagrams) before trusting a new VLM or alignment recipe; for kernel-tuning agents, gate every change on a correctness check and compare against your vendor-library baseline.

prior_narrative.tldr: Speculative decoding — verifying multiple draft tokens per step to cut inference latency — is now developing on two separate fronts: new drafting research and production serving guides. A mid-August paper (DARTree) pushed the research side toward diffusion-based draft trees that predict whole token blocks instead of single tokens.
prior_narrative.whats_new: A new paper (AsymSpec, Aug 26) targets speculative decoding specifically at agentic pipelines, arguing that generic techniques don't address the latency cost of long, tool-call-and-retrieval-inflated context that agents accumulate.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: If your agent pipeline is context-heavy (tool loops, retrieval, multi-turn memory), the generic speculative-decoding tuning already documented for production (vLLM/EAGLE-3/DFlash/DSpark) may not capture agent-specific savings — a context-aware variant like AsymSpec is what to watch for next.

beats.headline: DARTree proposes diffusion-based draft trees to cut proposal latency further
beats.summary: A diffusion drafter predicts an entire token block at once instead of one token at a time, aiming to reduce the latency of the draft step itself.

beats.headline: vLLM publishes a hands-on speculative-decoding tuning guide for AMD GPUs
beats.summary: The guide covers draft-and-verify mechanics and configuration across MTP, EAGLE-3, DFlash, and DSpark, with benchmark results — a practical reference for teams already running vLLM.

beats.headline: AsymSpec argues agentic LLM pipelines need context-asymmetric speculative decoding
beats.summary: Long accumulated context from retrieval, tool use, and multi-turn interaction inflates inference cost in ways generic speculative decoding and context-compression tricks don't fully address, the paper argues.

open_questions: Does AsymSpec's context-asymmetric approach get benchmarked against production serving stacks (vLLM/EAGLE-3/DFlash) rather than only academic baselines?
Is there a reference implementation of AsymSpec that agent-pipeline builders can actually try, or is it paper-only for now?
How much of DARTree's diffusion-drafting latency win holds up outside its own benchmark suite?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: Don't assume the generic speculative-decoding tuning already documented for vLLM (EAGLE-3/DFlash/DSpark) captures agent-specific savings — if your pipeline's context keeps growing from tool calls and retrieval, watch for a runnable implementation of context-asymmetric techniques like AsymSpec before investing engineering time.
